correctness.rationale: For every integer k>=2 and lambda strictly between 0 and 1, the 2k-point matching-contracted equilateral metric has range <=1. Strict convexity of the uniform variance on potentials modulo constants forces each maximizer to a tight-edge-connected polytope vertex. Every such vertex has six possible states per matched pair and both a lower/upper anchor. An opposite split-pair replacement raises variance by 2 lambda(1-lambda)/(2k); a same-side two-split randomized replacement raises expected variance by (k-1)lambda(1-lambda)/k^2. Hence at most one split pair maximizes. Pure states have variance a(k-a)/k^2. The one-split finite difference (k-2a-lambda-1)/k^2 is maximized at a=(k-1)/2 for odd k, with difference from the best pure state lambda[(2k-1)lambda-2(k-1)]/(4k^2). This yields precisely the stated parity law and transition lambda=2(k-1)/(2k-1), with both classes at the transition. Endpoints lambda=0,1 are intentionally excluded. Independent direct enumeration at 12 rational k/lambda instances corroborated but does not prove the infinite theorem.

evidence: Prior vertex theorem handles arbitrary n with k independently shortened pairs but has no variance functional, while equilateral spread fixes only the lambda=1 boundary.

value.rationale: The sharp Lipschitz-to-centered-L2 norm is a natural metric invariant. Equal contraction of disjoint pairs leads to a genuinely nontrivial parity obstruction and a sharp one-defect optimizer transition, distinguishing values continuously between equilateral and matched metrics. The one-split localization lemma and equality family are reusable structural facts, not merely a finite numerical sample.

limitations: The theorem does not apply to unequal atomic weights, overlapped shortening edges or lambda=1 optimizer equality family.
Finite cross-checks do not prove the quantified all-k, real-lambda statement.
